summary: Describes a common API for multicast that lets applications use the most efficient group-communication service available at runtime, even when multicast support varies across the Internet. It is an experimental document that addresses naming and addressing for such groups.

plainLanguage.summary: A single plug that works with whichever kind of wall socket is in the room, so apps need not care.

questions: how can apps use multicast everywhere
what is a common multicast api
subtitle: A single API that lets applications use whatever multicast is available, without rewriting code.

tldr.problem: Applications must choose between IPv4, IPv6, and overlay multicast at coding time. The standard socket API binds group names to specific technologies, forcing separate code paths for each deployment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7046 defines a common multicast API that separates group naming (application level) from addressing (technology level). Applications use multicast URIs; the system maps them at runtime to available technologies.
tldr.outcome: Experimental research specification. The HAMcast project implemented it; adoption in production systems remains limited.

facts.label: API call categories
facts.value: Group Management, Send/Receive, Socket Options, Service Calls

today: RFC 7046 is an Experimental specification from the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF). It has not been obsoleted or updated. The HAMcast project demonstrated the concept, but the API has seen limited adoption in mainstream systems. It remains a research contribution to multicast system design.

sections.title: The Multicast Technology Problem
sections.content:
Today's networks support multicast in multiple ways: IP multicast (IPv4 and IPv6), overlays, and application-layer schemes. Developers must decide at coding time which technologies to support and write separate code for each. If a network lacks native multicast, applications must fall back to unicast or use overlay multicast. There is no standard way to write code that runs everywhere and adapts to local conditions.

RFC 7046 defines a platform-level API and naming scheme that abstracts multicast from its implementation. Applications specify groups using technology-independent names (URIs); the system translates them to technology-specific addresses at runtime.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, you have to know whether your phone will use 4G or WiFi and write different code for each. Instead, your code should work with both automatically.

sections.title: Group Names, Group Addresses, and Namespaces
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes Group Names (application identifiers, independent of technology) from Group Addresses (routing identifiers specific to a technology). A Multicast Namespace is a collection of designators for groups that share syntax and semantics.

For example, the Group Name ham:ip:224.1.2.3:5000 (a multicast URI) can map to multiple Group Addresses depending on the available technologies: an IPv4 address in one domain, an IPv6 address in another, or an overlay hash in a pure-overlay network. The application always uses the Group Name; the system handles the translation.
sections.plainLanguage: The group name is 'News channel 5.' The group address is either an IPv4 number, an IPv6 number, or a hash, depending on what's available.

sections.title: Multicast URIs and Namespaces
sections.content:
Multicast URIs follow the syntax ham:namespace:group[@instantiation][:port][/credentials]. The namespace element specifies the syntax and semantics of the group identifier. Common namespaces are:

  • IP: IPv4 or IPv6 addresses or DNS names.
  • SHA-2: Hash digests for overlay multicast.
  • Opaque: Arbitrary strings without intrinsic meaning.
  • SIP: SIP conference URIs for VoIP multicast.
  • RELOAD: Peer-to-peer overlay identifiers.

The group identifies the multicast stream. The optional instantiation identifies the source or service instance. port selects an application at that instance. credentials encode security or AAA information.
sections.plainLanguage: A group name is like a mailing address: the namespace is the country, the group is the street, the instantiation is the building, the port is the apartment number.

sections.title: The Common Multicast API
sections.content:
The API provides four categories of calls:

  • Group Management: create (open a socket), join, leave, delete (close the socket). These manage multicast group membership.
  • Send/Receive: send and receive transfer data to and from a Group Name. The group name is returned with received data so applications can distinguish groups on one socket.
  • Socket Options: addInterface, delInterface, setTTL configure the socket for specific technologies or hop limits.
  • Service Calls: groupSet, parentSet, childrenSet provide information about local multicast state, useful for gateways and monitoring.

One socket can join multiple groups; the system handles all available technologies transparently.
sections.plainLanguage: The API is like opening a mailbox (create), joining a mailing list (join), sending a letter (send), reading mail (receive), and checking who's in the list (groupSet).

sections.title: Hybrid Multicast Gateways
sections.content:
The API enables inter-domain multicast gateways that bridge different technologies. A gateway can receive multicast data on one Interface (e.g., IPv6) and forward it on another (e.g., overlay multicast) while maintaining a coherent view of Group Names and group membership across domains.

Service calls like designatedHost, parentSet, and childrenSet let gateways query local multicast forwarding state. neighborSet returns the set of neighbors seen by a multicast routing protocol. Membership events notify gateways when peers join or leave a group on any Interface.
sections.plainLanguage: A translator at the border between networks. It hears a message in one language (IPv4) and repeats it in another (overlay). It knows which neighbors are listening on each side.

sections.title: HAMcast Implementation
sections.content:
The RFC documents an open-source reference implementation: HAMcast (Hybrid Adaptive Multicast). It provides C++ and Java libraries implementing the API, a middleware service that manages group communication across multiple technologies, and pluggable multicast modules (IPv4, IPv6, overlays, etc.). The middleware discovers available Interfaces, maps Group Names to Group Addresses per technology, and bridges data between domains.

HAMcast validated the API design through real-world deployment, leading to refinements of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A real program that does all this. You can download it, use the library, and extend it with new multicast technologies.
